Here are verse-by-verse notes on Ezra 5, drawn from the sources found:

---

## Ezra 5 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 1
**"Later, the prophets Haggai and Zechariah son of Iddo prophesied to the Jews in Judah and Jerusalem in the name of the God of Israel, who was over them."**

- **The historical situation.** After 16 years of stalled work (from about 536 to 520 B.C.), the people had grown apathetic. Haggai and Zechariah appeared "at a time of deep depression," not on the crest of a revival (Adeney, cited by Guzik). The work had been stopped by Samaritan opposition and a decree from Artaxerxes (really the Pseudo-Smerdis), and the people had turned to building their own comfortable homes (Haggai 1:4). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-5/

- **The content of their prophesying.** Haggai's message was a direct rebuke: the people said "the time has not come" to rebuild the temple, but their real problem was misplaced priorities — they had "paneled houses" while God's house lay in ruins (Haggai 1:2-4). He called them to "consider your ways" and get to work (Haggai 1:7-8). Zechariah's prophecy was complementary: his name means "The LORD Remembers," and he focused on God's care for the people themselves, not only the building. He kept the coming Messiah before their minds. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-5/

- **"In the name of the God of Israel, who was over them."** This phrase verifies a renewed covenant relationship between the returned exiles and God. The prophets spoke with divine authority, not their own. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-5-commentary (citing Bob Utley)

- **Gill** notes that the prophets spoke "against them" (as some translators take the Hebrew), reproving them for sloth and for being intimidated by the Persian decree, which only forbade building the city walls, not the temple or their own houses. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/5.htm

- **The Pulpit Commentary** observes that the great political revolution in Persia — the overthrow of the Pseudo-Smerdis and the rise of Darius — failed to stir the people. A whole year passed with no action until Haggai suddenly appeared in the sixth month of Darius's second year. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezra-5.html

- **Zechariah "son of Iddo"** is actually the grandson of Iddo (Zechariah 1:1 says his father was Berechiah). Berechiah probably died young, so Zechariah was raised by Iddo and referred to as his son. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezra-5.html

---

### v. 2
**"Then Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and Jeshua son of Jozadak rose up and began to rebuild the house of God in Jerusalem. And the prophets of God were with them, helping them."**

- **"Rose up."** This Aramaic verb means to arise out of inactivity. Both leaders had apparently become passive along with the people. The preaching of the prophets, accompanied by the Spirit of God, "stirred up" their spirits (Haggai 1:14). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/5.htm

- **The prophets "helping them."** This means more than just prophesying. Haggai and Zechariah took a hand in the practical work of building. Their help included direct commands ("Go up to the mountain and bring wood," Haggai 1:8), warnings about divine judgment for neglect, exhortations ("Be strong … and work," Haggai 2:4), and encouraging predictions ("The hands of Zerubbabel … shall also finish it," Zechariah 4:9). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezra-5.html

- **Piper** emphasizes that God responded to the discouragement of His people by raising up prophets to speak His word into the situation. The result was that leaders "arose and began to rebuild." God's word through Haggai and Zechariah gave courage. — https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/take-courage-you-build-more-than-you-see

- **Timing.** The work resumed on the 24th day of the sixth month of Darius's second year — September 21, 520 B.C. — https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/take-courage-you-build-more-than-you-see

---

### v. 3
**"At that time Tattenai the governor of the region west of the Euphrates, Shethar-bozenai, and their associates went to the Jews and asked, 'Who authorized you to rebuild this temple and restore this structure?'"**

- **Who was Tattenai?** He was the Persian governor (pechah) of the entire province "Beyond the River" (west of the Euphrates), making him Zerubbabel's superior — Zerubbabel was governor (pechah) only of Judah. His name and office appear in a Babylonian record dated 502 B.C. speaking of "Ta-at[-tan-ni] governor of Ebernari." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-5/ (citing Kidner)

- **Why the challenge now?** Tattenai was likely acting on legitimate concerns, not Samaritan instigation. The Persian Empire had gone through severe political upheaval: Cambyses had died, the Pseudo-Smerdis (Gaumata) had usurped the throne, and Darius had only recently consolidated power after putting down multiple rebellions. Any large building project in a province could be preparation for revolt. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezra-5.html (Constable)

- **A different tone from earlier opposition.** Unlike Rehum and Shimshai in Ezra 4, Tattenai did not bring armed force to stop the work. He "seems to have been a mild and judicious man" (Clarke, cited by Guzik). He investigated rather than attacked. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-5/

- **"This wall" or "this structure."** The question concerns the temple walls specifically, not the city wall. Gill observes that by this time the builders had raised the temple walls to some visible height, which triggered the inquiry. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/5.htm

---

### v. 4
**"They also asked, 'What are the names of the men who are constructing this building?'"**

- **A compressed narrative.** Ellicott notes the text is compressed. Verse 10 makes clear the purpose: the authorities wanted the names of the chief promoters "to make them responsible" — effectively to have a list of people to hold accountable if the building proved seditious. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezra/5.htm (via search excerpt)

- **Gill** explains the Jews made "no scruple of telling them who they were; neither ashamed of their masters nor of their work, nor afraid of any ill consequences." They were not hiding anything. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/5.htm

- **Textual issue.** Some manuscripts (LXX) read "Then said they unto them" rather than "Then said we unto them," which seems more logical — it was Tattenai and his colleagues asking, not the Jews. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezra-5.html

- **The purpose was intimidation.** Bob Utley notes that asking for names was "for the purpose of intimidation and fear directed towards the Jewish leadership." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-5-commentary

---

### v. 5
**"But the eye of their God was on the elders of the Jews, so that they were not stopped until a report was sent to Darius and written instructions about this matter were returned."**

- **"The eye of their God."** This is an anthropomorphic idiom for God's attentive presence, care, and protection. It echoes Psalm 32:8, 33:18, 34:15, and 2 Chronicles 16:9 ("the eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth"). God watched over the elders "with a jealous watchfulness, which never for a moment slackens." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezra-5.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/5.htm

- **Morgan** adds: "We are not to suppose for a moment that this was something new. That eye had always been upon them, but through the teaching of the prophets … their consciousness of relationship to God had again been renewed." — Cited at https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-5/

- **Not stopped.** Unlike the earlier incident in Ezra 4:23 where work was forcibly halted, here Tattenai did not use force. The work continued even while the inquiry was pending — a delay of perhaps four to five months for the round trip to Babylon and back. This bought critical time. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-5/

- **Providential.** The fact that Tattenai "acceded to such a request rather than exercise his immediate authority one way or the other, was in itself somewhat remarkable" (Morgan). God's hand was on the Persian officials as well as on the Jewish elders. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-5/

- **Precept Austin** draws the application: "The eye of the enemy and the eye of God are continually upon us in all the work of life" (Joseph Parker). Knowing the eye of God is on us helps us persevere. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-5-commentary

---

### v. 6
**"This is the text of the letter that Tattenai the governor of the region west of the Euphrates, Shethar-bozenai, and their associates, the officials in the region, sent to King Darius."**

- **A preserved copy.** As a good administrator, Tattenai kept a copy of his letter, which Ezra later obtained and included in his record. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-5/

- **"The Apharsachites"** (KJV) — The Pulpit Commentary suggests this term may be a provincial variant of "Parsaya" (Persian) and may refer to actual Persians who formed the bodyguard and train of Tattenai and Shethar-bozenai. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezra-5.html

- **Contrast with Ezra 4.** Constable points out the difference between this letter and the one in Ezra 4:11-16 from Rehum and Shimshai. That earlier letter distorted the truth, painted the Jews as rebels, and demanded the work be stopped. Tattenai's letter is factually accurate and requests only verification. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezra-5.html

---

### v. 7
**"The report they sent him read as follows: To King Darius: All peace."**

- **Standard Persian greeting.** "All peace" (Aramaic: *shelema kol*) was the conventional salutation in official Persian correspondence, equivalent to wishing the king total well-being. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/5.htm

---

### v. 8
**"Let it be known to the king that we went into the province of Judah, to the house of the great God. The people are rebuilding it with large stones, and placing timbers in the walls. This work is being carried out diligently and is prospering in their hands."**

- **"The house of the great God."** This is a remarkable phrase on the lips of a pagan Persian official. The Pulpit Commentary says it indicates the general Persian belief that the God of the Jews was indeed a great deity. Persian Zoroastrians acknowledged a supreme god (Ahura Mazda), and they seem to have identified YHWH with Him. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezra-5.html

- **"Large stones" — literally "stones of rolling."** These were stones so large they had to be rolled into place. However, the Pulpit Commentary notes that dressed stones were not rolled but dragged on sledges. The LXX translates "choice stones"; the Vulgate "unpolished or rough stones"; some Jewish expositors suggest "marble." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezra-5.html

- **"Timbers … in the walls."** Kidner notes this was a common construction feature in the ancient Near East: courses of timber between stone or brick, possibly as earthquake reinforcement. This was also a feature of Solomon's original temple (1 Kings 6:36). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-5/

- **"Diligently and prospering."** Tattenai reports the work is going fast and successfully — an objective, unembellished observation. He was not trying to make the Jews look bad. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-5/

---

### v. 9–10
**"So we questioned the elders and asked, 'Who authorized you to rebuild this temple and restore this structure?' We also asked for their names, so that we could write down the names of their leaders for your information."**

- **Recapping the earlier encounter.** These verses repeat and expand on vv. 3-4, now in Tattenai's own words to the king. He is transparent about what he did and why. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-5/

- **For accountability.** The purpose of asking names was to "certify" (inform officially) the king exactly who the leaders were, so they could be held responsible if necessary. This was standard Persian administrative procedure, not necessarily hostile. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/5.htm

---

### v. 11
**"And this is the answer they returned: 'We are servants of the God of heaven and earth, and we are rebuilding the temple that was built many years ago, which a great king of Israel built and completed.'"**

- **"Servants of the God of heaven and earth."** The elders decline to give a list of individual names. Instead they merge their identities: "As individuals, we are nothing … what we do, we do simply as servants of God." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezra-5.html

- **"God of heaven and earth"** — a rare title in the Old Testament. Merrill notes it was important "against the background of rampant polytheism or even the dualism of newly emerging Zoroastrianism … to affirm that Yahweh is Lord of all in heaven and on earth." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezra-5.html

- **Fensham adds** that "the God of heaven" was probably an attempt to create sympathy at the Persian court, because Ahura Mazda was also regarded as "god of the heaven" and creator of heaven and earth. The Jews used Persian religious language to build a bridge. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezra-5.html

- **"A great king of Israel."** This refers to Solomon, who built the first temple about 400 years earlier — a king great in wisdom, wealth, and extent of kingdom. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/5.htm

- **Precept Austin** observes that the Jews gave a "strong witness" about God and His covenant faithfulness. They let Tattenai know who they served and why. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-5-commentary

---

### v. 12
**"'But since our fathers angered the God of heaven, He delivered them into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, the Chaldean who destroyed this temple and carried away the people to Babylon.'"**

- **Honest confession of sin.** The Jewish elders do not blame Nebuchadnezzar or political circumstances. They openly acknowledge that the destruction of the temple was divine judgment for their fathers' idolatry. The Pulpit Commentary details the "long series of idolatries" including child sacrifice, Baal worship, and the pollutions of the Dea Syra, for which God used Nebuchadnezzar as His instrument of chastisement. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezra-5.html

- **Theological honesty before pagans.** The Jews made no attempt to spin their history. They admitted their nation's sin and God's righteous judgment, which gave credibility to their claim about Cyrus's decree. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/5.htm

---

### v. 13
**"'In his first year, however, Cyrus king of Babylon issued a decree to rebuild this house of God.'"**

- **"Cyrus king of Babylon."** This title is confirmed by recently discovered contract tablets showing Cyrus bore the title "king of Babylon" from the date of his conquest. His successors — Cambyses, Darius, and even Artaxerxes — continued using it. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezra-5.html

- **The pivot from judgment to restoration.** The elders' narrative moves directly from the destruction under Nebuchadnezzar to the decree of Cyrus, showing God's sovereignty over history and His faithfulness to restore. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-5/

---

### v. 14–15
**"'He also removed from the temple of Babylon the gold and silver articles belonging to the house of God, which Nebuchadnezzar had taken and carried there from the temple in Jerusalem. King Cyrus gave these articles to a man named Sheshbazzar, whom he appointed governor and instructed, "Take these articles, put them in the temple in Jerusalem, and let the house of God be rebuilt on its original site."'"**

- **The temple articles.** These were highly significant — tangible evidence both of the conquest (to Babylonians) and of the disgrace (to Jews). Their retention was a perpetual desecration; their return by Cyrus was "an act at once of piety and of kindliness." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezra-5.html (citing Ezra 1:7-11)

- **Who is Sheshbazzar?** This is a debated identity. Gill and many traditional commentators identify Sheshbazzar with Zerubbabel himself, since both are said to have "laid the foundation" (cf. Zechariah 4:9). The name "Sheshbazzar" would be the one appearing in Persian records, making it the right name to cite to Darius. Others (Yamauchi, cited by Guzik) suggest Sheshbazzar was the official Persian-appointed "governor" while Zerubbabel was the popular leader. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-5/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/5.htm

- **"On its original site."** The temple was to be rebuilt on the same holy ground where Abraham offered Isaac (in a figure, Hebrews 11:17-19), where the angel stayed the pestilence in David's time (2 Samuel 24:16-18), and where the glory of the Lord filled Solomon's temple (2 Chronicles 7:1). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezra-5.html

---

### v. 16
**"'So this Sheshbazzar came and laid the foundation of the house of God in Jerusalem, and from that time until now it has been under construction, but it has not yet been completed.'"**

- **"From that time until now."** This summary skips over the long interruption. The Pulpit Commentary suggests this may be Tattenai's own statement rather than the Jews' words — he may not have known about the 16-year gap. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezra-5.html

- **Gill** notes the time span: from Cyrus's first year to Darius's second year was about 18 years, with work going on "slowly, not without interruption and intermission, through the enmity of the Samaritans." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/5.htm

- **Bob Utley** notes that Sheshbazzar "cleared off the rubble and found the original foundations, but the temple itself was not rebuilt until the second return under Zerubbabel and Jeshua." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-5-commentary

---

### v. 17
**"'Now, therefore, if it pleases the king, let a search be made of the royal archives in Babylon to see if King Cyrus did indeed issue a decree to rebuild the house of God in Jerusalem. Then let the king send us his decision in this matter.'"**

- **The archives.** The "king's treasure house" (KJV) or "royal archives" refers to the record chambers attached to Persian royal residences. The Vulgate translates "the king's library." Ancient Near Eastern kings kept extensive archives; some of these have been discovered by archaeologists (e.g., Layard's discovery of Asshur-bani-pal's library at Koyunjik in 1850, and a cache of 3,000–4,000 tablets near Babylon in 1875-76). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezra-5.html

- **The Pulpit Commentary** intriguingly notes: "It is quite possible that the 'decree of Cyrus' may still exist, and be one day recovered." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezra-5.html

- **Tattenai's fairness.** He does not ask Darius to stop the work or punish the Jews. He simply requests verification. This stands in stark contrast to the earlier letter from Rehum and Shimshai, which was full of accusations and demanded immediate action. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezra-5.html

- **Morgan** comments: Tattenai "either did not believe that such a decree had ever been promulgated, or considered that it could not be found" — yet he allowed the matter to be settled by evidence, not force. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-5/

- **The decree was not found in Babylon.** When the search was made (Ezra 6), the original was eventually located not in Babylon but at Ecbatana (Achmetha), the Persian summer capital — a detail that underscores the historical authenticity of the account. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezra-5.html

---

## Points of Particular Interest

### Sheshbazzar vs. Zerubbabel
Traditional older commentators (Gill) identify Sheshbazzar with Zerubbabel as one person under two names. More recent evangelical scholars (Yamauchi, Constable) regard Sheshbazzar as the first Persian-appointed governor who began the work, with Zerubbabel as the popular leader who later completed it. Both views appear in the commentaries surveyed. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/5.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-5/

### God's Sovereignty and Human Means
A theme running through multiple sources: God used prophets (Haggai and Zechariah), leaders (Zerubbabel and Jeshua), the community of returned exiles, and even pagan Persian officials (Tattenai and Darius) to accomplish His purpose. Precept Austin cites Breneman: "In order to fulfill his purpose, God used and coordinated the preaching of the prophets, the work of the leaders, the determination of the whole community, and the decisions of 'pagan' government officials." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-5-commentary

### The "God of Heaven and Earth" Title
This title appears to be a deliberate bridge to Persian Zoroastrian thought. Fensham notes that the Jews' use of "the God of heaven" was "probably an attempt … to create sympathy for their cause in the Persian court, because Ahuramazda, the Persian god, was also regarded as 'god of the heaven.'" — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezra-5.html

### Denominational Distinctives
Among the sources surveyed, no sharp denominational disagreements surfaced on Ezra 5. The chapter is largely narrative, and the traditional Protestant commentators (Baptist Gill, Reformed-leaning Constable, charismatic Guzik, Reformed Baptist Piper) read it in substantially the same way — as an account of God's providential care, the power of prophetic preaching to revive God's work, and the integrity of faithful witness before governing authorities. No distinctly Catholic, Orthodox, or modern critical commentary was located in the search results.

---

*Sources: Enduring Word (Guzik), Gill's Exposition, Pulpit Commentary, Ellicott's Commentary, Constable's Expository Notes, Precept Austin (compilation), Desiring God (Piper).*
